doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: First record date for Chiaroscuro with Bob Wilber
summary: Wilber heard them at Condon's and organised the first record with the Hamilton quartet; Flanigan criticises its direct-pickup sound.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Well when did the first record date come about?

That was something that Bob Wilber instigated for the Chiaroscuro label. He heard us play at Eddie Condon’s and he was blown away that all these young guys — we were all under 25 then I guess — were playing this style music, so he got a date and he put — the original quartet, which was without piano, just Flory on guitar, Riggs on drums, myself and Hamilton, and with the addition of Wilber on soprano and alto and clarinet, but one at a time thankfully.
Yeah. That would be a little Roland Kirky.

Roland Kirky. Quirky and Kirky. So I wasn’t terrifically — I guess at the time I thought it was okay, but these days, a typical seventies product with the direct pick-up sound into the board, and no microphone on the bass, direct off the guitar and no putting a mic on the amplifier or anything. It was just a cruddy recording. All the new technologies come out, like the pick-ups and the direct boxes and all this kind of stuff, so the techies figure they’ve got to use them. But now all the best recording were made before that, and now there are a number of people who have had the realization that we should go back there and see some high end and/or good recordings coming out with a more acoustical nature. Christian McBride for one, records mostly acoustically. I don’t believe I’ve ever heard a record of his that had a direct pick-up sound on it, thank goodness.
